analysis.one_liner: Counts veterans' education benefits as federal funds, closing a loophole for-profit colleges use to bypass the 90/10 rule.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or hearing and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires for-profit colleges to get at least 10% of their revenue from sources other than federal student aid — the "90/10 rule" — so schools that depend on federal money for nearly all their income can lose it. Current law does not count veterans' education benefits (GI Bill and Defense Department tuition assistance) as federal money, so some schools target veterans to collect that revenue while staying technically under the cap. This bill would count veterans' benefits as federal money, cutting off both federal student aid and all Defense and VA education funds from any for-profit school that fails the test.
analysis.who_benefits: Veterans and active-duty service members, who would stop being a revenue target for schools that exceed the federal-funding dependence cap, plus taxpayers who fund the GI Bill and tuition assistance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Veterans and service members using education benefits

how_it_helps.text: Counts veterans' education benefits toward the 90/10 rule, so a for-profit college can no longer use GI Bill and military tuition assistance money to satisfy the requirement that 10% of its revenue come from outside federal aid.

Makes a for-profit school that fails the 90/10 rule ineligible not just for federal student aid but also for all Defense Department and Veterans Affairs education assistance, closing the fallback the old rule left open.
Requires the Education Department to notify Defense and Veterans Affairs when a school loses or regains eligibility, so the other departments can actually cut off funds.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges that lean heavily on veterans' benefits for revenue; if the rule pushes any of them out of business, their enrolled students could lose credits or completion of programs they paid for.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit colleges dependent on veteran benefits

drawbacks.text: The penalty is severe and automatic: a school that slips below the threshold loses federal student aid and all VA and Defense education funds at once, and an abrupt shutdown could strand enrolled students mid-program without their credits transferring.

Pressure on the 90% side of the ledger can push schools to chase other non-federal revenue — such as private loans to students — rather than reduce costs, shifting the burden rather than fixing the underlying problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and well-documented problem: for-profit colleges recruiting veterans aggressively because GI Bill money did not count under the 90/10 rule. The protection for veterans and taxpayers outweighs the business cost to schools that cannot survive without federal dollars, though the all-or-nothing cutoff could hurt students at a failing school through no fault of their own. As a narrow rule change with only three cosponsors, it was modest in scope.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2011 and split among three committees and their subcommittees, and none of them took it up before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on December 20, 2011, near the end of the first session of the 112th Congress.
Three House Democrats cosponsored it; no Republicans did.

The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs committees, which in early 2012 routed pieces of it to the Economic Opportunity, Military Personnel, and Higher Education subcommittees.
No committee or subcommittee held a markup, hearing, or vote, and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges that recruit veterans kept the existing 90/10 loophole, so the GI Bill and tuition assistance money they depend on continued to flow without the new limit.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to count veterans' education benefits under the 90/10 rule.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and sent it to subcommittees, but never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied to keep veterans' benefits excluded from the 90/10 rule during this period; the exemption the bill targeted remained in place.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no roll calls show the split; all four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill would count GI Bill and military tuition assistance money against the 90/10 cap, ending the ability of schools to exceed the federal-dependence limit by collecting veterans' benefits. Schools that cannot meet the cap with other revenue would lose federal aid and all VA and Defense education funds, cutting off a revenue stream built largely on veterans' federal dollars. The exemption it targeted stayed in place.

industries.industry: Taxpayers funding VA and Defense education benefits
industries.note: Veterans' benefits money would stop counting as the non-federal 10%, reducing the use of GI Bill and tuition assistance funds at schools already overly dependent on federal aid.
